lesson.title: The missing payment response
lesson.text: A ₹1,200 payment commits, but the response times out. The client sends the same request again. What happens to the ledger?

lesson.title: Why a lookup can fail
lesson.text: A blind retry can charge twice. Checking for a prior payment before writing also races when two requests see an empty result.

lesson.title: Claim the intent and commit once
lesson.text: Keep one client-generated key per intent. Scope it to tenant and operation and compare a canonical payload fingerprint. Use a database unique constraint to arbitrate concurrent attempts. Commit the effect and recorded response in one transaction, then replay the result on a matching retry.

lesson.title: Defend the external boundary
lesson.text: Persist an intent and outbox together. Reuse a stable provider key on delivery. Reconcile ambiguous outcomes through provider lookup or verified events. Align key retention with your retry contract.

cards.prompt: A payment request times out. What can you infer about its outcome?
cards.answer: The outcome is unknown. The write might already have committed. Retry using the same operation key and resolve against the recorded result.

cards.prompt: Why can two requests both pass an existence check?
cards.answer: Both may read before either writes. Use an atomic claim backed by a unique constraint, and commit the ledger effect with the replay record.

cards.prompt: The provider might have charged before a worker crashed. How do you recover?
cards.answer: Reconcile using the stable provider key, a lookup or a verified event. Check provider retention before considering a retry. Preserve unresolved intents for investigation.

lesson.title: Predict what happens
lesson.text: A promotion drives thousands of reads per second for the same product. The database is already close to capacity. What happens when the cache entry expires?

lesson.title: Where the simple design breaks
lesson.text: Cache-aside reduces repeated reads, but a hot key expiring can send many simultaneous misses to the database. Identical expiration times amplify this across keys.

lesson.title: Change the architecture
lesson.text: Read from the cache first. On a miss, let one request per key refill it within a bounded deadline. Add jitter across expirations and enforce a database concurrency budget.

lesson.title: Defend the trade-off
lesson.text: Define a staleness budget by field. Descriptions may tolerate stale-while-revalidate. Checkout should validate price against its authoritative source. Cache invalidation can race with an older in-flight fill, so use versions where stale rewrites matter.

cards.prompt: Why can a cache increase database load at expiry?
cards.answer: Many requests observe the same miss and refill concurrently.

cards.prompt: How do you handle a hot-key stampede?
cards.answer: Coalesce fills per key, bound refill concurrency and consider serving stale data within policy.

cards.prompt: Would you use the same policy for descriptions and checkout prices?
cards.answer: Choose separate staleness budgets and validate the final price against the authoritative service.

lesson.title: Predict what happens
lesson.text: An integration sends 500 requests in one second after reconnecting. You want to allow short bursts while protecting other tenants. Where would you enforce the limit?

lesson.title: Where the simple design breaks
lesson.text: A fixed-window counter permits requests near the end of one window and again at the start of the next. A counter per gateway instance also multiplies the effective limit as the fleet scales.

lesson.title: Change the architecture
lesson.text: Use a token bucket per tenant. Refill at a configured rate up to a burst capacity and debit atomically in a shared store when enforcing a global budget. Return 429 with retry guidance when depleted.

lesson.title: Defend the trade-off
lesson.text: A shared limiter adds latency and an availability dependency. Decide per endpoint whether to fail closed or admit a bounded amount through a local emergency budget. Plan for hot tenant keys.

cards.prompt: What happens at a fixed-window boundary?
cards.answer: A client can spend two windows of quota in a short interval.

cards.prompt: Which two values define token-bucket behavior?
cards.answer: Refill rate governs sustained throughput and capacity bounds the available burst.

cards.prompt: The shared limiter fails. What policy should you defend?
cards.answer: Tie fail-open or fail-closed behavior to endpoint risk and apply a bounded local fallback if admitting traffic.

lesson.title: Predict what happens
lesson.text: Search requests range from 20 ms to several seconds. Traffic is spread evenly by request count, yet some workers are overloaded. Why?

lesson.title: Where the simple design breaks
lesson.text: Round robin equalizes assignment counts. Long requests can overlap on one worker and exhaust its concurrency budget while other workers are idle.

lesson.title: Change the architecture
lesson.text: Use in-flight work as a routing signal where available, and bound concurrency per worker. Remove unhealthy endpoints from rotation and drain connections before planned shutdown.

lesson.title: Defend the trade-off
lesson.text: Health checks can oscillate during overload. Use bounded retries, readiness hysteresis and load shedding. A global retry burst can overload the healthy remainder during a partial outage.

cards.prompt: Why does equal request count fail to equalize load?
cards.answer: Requests occupy resources for different durations and may have different cost.

cards.prompt: What is connection draining for?
cards.answer: Stop sending new work to an endpoint while letting existing work finish within a deadline.

cards.prompt: Why can removing unhealthy endpoints trigger cascading failure?
cards.answer: Remaining capacity drops while retries increase effective load. Shed work and cap retries.

lesson.title: Predict what happens
lesson.text: A user signs up and email delivery takes several seconds. How can the API respond quickly while keeping the notification reliable?

lesson.title: Where the simple design breaks
lesson.text: A synchronous call ties signup latency to the email provider. Publishing after committing signup leaves a failure window where the account exists but no notification was queued.

lesson.title: Change the architecture
lesson.text: Commit the account and an outbox row together. Publish asynchronously. Consumers acknowledge after processing and use stable message IDs to deduplicate effects where supported.

lesson.title: Defend the trade-off
lesson.text: Retries can overwhelm a slow provider. Use backoff, attempt limits, dead-letter handling and queue age alerts. A provider timeout after sending requires reconciliation or a provider-supported idempotency contract.

cards.prompt: Can an outbox relay deliver an event twice?
cards.answer: Yes. A publish can succeed before the relay records progress, so a later attempt can publish again.

cards.prompt: Which metric catches delayed delivery even when producers look healthy?
cards.answer: Age of the oldest pending message or end-to-end delivery delay, monitored against the delivery objective.

lesson.title: Predict what happens
lesson.text: A growing event store no longer fits comfortably on one database. One customer generates half of all writes. What happens if you hash by tenant?

lesson.title: Where the simple design breaks
lesson.text: Hashing tenant IDs distributes tenants. All events for one tenant still land on a single shard, so a hot customer can exhaust that shard independently of fleet capacity.

lesson.title: Change the architecture
lesson.text: Choose a key from query and write patterns. Tenant-local reads favor tenant partitioning. Bucket the busiest tenants across shards if the dominant problem is write skew.

lesson.title: Defend the trade-off
lesson.text: Bucketing trades write throughput for query fan-out and complicates ordering. Define an ordering scope, plan resumable backfills, and compare shadow reads before switching a routing map.

cards.prompt: Why can hashing still produce a hot shard?
cards.answer: Hashing balances keys, while request volume can be concentrated on a single key.

cards.prompt: What does bucketing a busy tenant change?
cards.answer: Writes spread across buckets, while tenant-wide reads may query and merge multiple buckets.

cards.prompt: What must a resharding plan specify?
cards.answer: Routing ownership, backfill and catch-up, read verification, cutover and recovery if migration stalls.

lesson.title: When a dependency stalls
lesson.text: A checkout service asks a recommendations API for optional product suggestions. The dependency starts taking seconds to respond. Checkout workers fill up even though the order database is healthy. Where would you cut the failure path?

lesson.title: What timeouts leave behind
lesson.text: A timeout limits one call. Under sustained failure, incoming requests can still spend their entire timeout waiting, and retries can increase load on the struggling dependency. Bound concurrency and stop sending most calls while the dependency is unhealthy.

lesson.title: Open the circuit and test recovery
lesson.text: In the closed state, forward calls and measure eligible failures over a rolling window. Open after a minimum sample and failure threshold are met. While open, fail fast or omit optional recommendations. After a cooldown, move to half-open and allow a bounded number of probes. Close after sufficient successful probes, or reopen when probes fail.

lesson.title: Set boundaries and protect correctness
lesson.text: Scope the circuit to a dependency operation or failure domain. Exclude caller errors from the failure count and combine the breaker with deadlines and a concurrency limit. Omit optional recommendations safely. If payment authorization is unavailable, surface the unavailable or unknown outcome according to the payment contract. Track state changes, rejected calls, probe outcomes and checkout latency.

cards.prompt: Why can checkout still slow down when every downstream call has a timeout?
cards.answer: During sustained failure, many simultaneous calls can each wait up to the timeout. A circuit breaker rejects most calls quickly after detecting failures, while a concurrency limit caps outstanding work.

cards.prompt: Why does the breaker limit calls in the half-open state?
cards.answer: A small set of probes tests recovery without sending the full backlog. Probe success can close the circuit and a failed probe can reopen it.

cards.prompt: Can checkout use the same fallback for recommendations and payment authorization?
cards.answer: Recommendations are optional and can be omitted. Payment authorization has a correctness requirement, so checkout must follow the payment contract for unavailable or unknown outcomes.

cards.answer: A single destructive schema change can break old instances immediately. Expand first so both versions can operate during the rollout, then remove compatibility structures later.

lesson.text: An inventory database and an order database must either both commit a reservation or both abort. What happens if the coordinator disappears between their decisions?

lesson.title: Understand prepare and commit
lesson.text: The coordinator first asks every participant to prepare. A prepared participant durably records its promise and retains the resources needed to commit. Only after every required participant votes yes does the coordinator durably decide commit.

lesson.title: Implement durable coordination
lesson.text: Use a transaction manager and participants that implement the same supported protocol. Persist transaction identity and the coordinator decision before announcing commit. Participants must make repeated commit or abort messages safe and recover unresolved transactions from durable logs.

lesson.title: Recover an uncertain participant
lesson.text: A participant that voted yes cannot safely abort merely because its timer expires: the coordinator may already have committed elsewhere. It remains in doubt until it recovers the authoritative decision, potentially holding locks and reducing availability.

lesson.title: One slow replica dominates the user experience
lesson.text: A read-only profile lookup normally takes 20 ms, but occasional replicas take 800 ms during storage pauses. A page fans out to ten lookups and waits for all of them. Even when each lookup is usually fast, one straggler can dominate page latency. How can the caller reduce this tail without doubling all traffic?

lesson.title: Race a delayed second read
lesson.text: Send the initial read normally. If it remains incomplete beyond a measured threshold, send one hedge to a different eligible replica. Accept the first valid successful response and cancel the other attempt. This differs from waiting for the original attempt to fail: both may be in flight. Replica selection should avoid the same overloaded host or shared failure domain.

lesson.title: Bound the extra work
lesson.text: Choose the hedge delay from measured latency distributions, for example near the normal p95, then validate it under realistic load. Give both attempts the same end-to-end deadline. Enforce one extra attempt maximum and a fleet-wide hedge concurrency or traffic budget. Preserve the original request identity in traces and separately record attempt identity, hedge launch, winning attempt and cancellation outcome.

lesson.title: Prevent load feedback and inconsistent answers
lesson.text: During a broad slowdown, many requests cross the threshold simultaneously. Disable or throttle hedges when capacity is constrained rather than amplifying the outage. Cancellation may arrive after expensive work has finished, so count actual backend work. A second replica must satisfy the same freshness and authorization requirements. The first response is usable only if it meets the requested version or consistency contract. A fast error should not automatically beat a still-pending valid response.

lesson.title: Choose workloads where duplication is safe
lesson.text: Use hedging for bounded, replay-safe reads with genuinely independent latency variation and spare capacity. Side-effecting operations require a separate safe deduplication contract and are usually poor initial candidates. Compare p99 latency benefit with incremental backend CPU, network traffic and connection occupancy. If all replicas share one saturated disk tier, moving work between them may provide little benefit.

lesson.title: Follow the two racing paths
lesson.text: The coordinator starts the primary read. The delay gate opens only if that read is still pending and the hedge budget permits another attempt. It sends the hedge to an independent replica. The coordinator accepts the first response that meets the read contract and cancels remaining work. During overload, the gate stays closed and the caller relies on its deadline and normal overload policy.

cards.prompt: Why delay the second attempt instead of duplicating every read immediately?
cards.answer: Most reads finish normally before the delay. A delayed hedge targets stragglers while reducing duplicate work. The threshold must be measured and constrained by an extra-work budget.

cards.prompt: What happens if every read becomes slow during a shared storage incident?
cards.answer: Many hedges can launch together and amplify load without finding an independent fast path. Throttle or disable hedges under saturation and retain the original deadline.

cards.prompt: Can the caller accept whichever replica responds first?
cards.answer: Only a valid successful response satisfying the requested consistency and freshness contract can win. A stale replica or fast error must not bypass those requirements.

lesson.title: Find divergence without copying everything
lesson.text: Two replicas store a billion keys after a network interruption. Most records match, but a small fraction differ. Comparing or copying every value would consume substantial bandwidth. How can replicas locate the changed ranges efficiently?

lesson.title: Summarize ranges recursively
lesson.text: A Merkle tree hashes records into leaves and combines child hashes into parent hashes. Replicas with identical tree shape, record ordering and hash encoding compare root hashes. Matching roots indicate matching represented content under the hash assumptions. If roots differ, compare child hashes and descend only into mismatching branches.

lesson.title: Make comparisons reproducible
lesson.text: Partition the same keyspace into deterministic ranges. Canonically encode keys, values, versions and deletion markers before hashing. Build summaries from a consistent snapshot or a documented stable generation. Exchange generation identity and root hashes, then recursively request mismatching child summaries until reaching ranges small enough to exchange records. Verify repaired ranges again after applying changes.

lesson.title: Resolve versions before repairing data
lesson.text: A hash mismatch identifies divergence but does not tell which copy is authoritative. Apply the store’s version or conflict-resolution rules to differing records. Include tombstones so a replica cannot resurrect a deleted record. Retain deletion information long enough for supported offline replicas, or require a full resynchronization when they exceed that window. A moving dataset can keep changing roots, so compare stable generations and catch up subsequent writes separately.

lesson.title: Budget background repair
lesson.text: Merkle summaries trade CPU, metadata storage and tree-maintenance work for lower network comparison cost when most ranges match. Coarse leaves require larger range transfers, while fine leaves increase metadata. Throttle repair I/O and prioritize ranges with known divergence. Measure repair age, bytes compared and transferred, conflicting versions and convergence failures.

lesson.title: Walk through a mismatching branch
lesson.text: The repair coordinator requests snapshot summaries from both replicas. It compares roots and descends into mismatching ranges. The version resolver inspects records from those ranges and selects valid merged or newer versions according to the store contract. During a failed transfer, resume from the stable generation and recheck the repaired range. Deletion markers travel with records and remain part of the resulting hash.

cards.prompt: How does a Merkle tree avoid transferring all replica records during comparison?
cards.answer: Compare roots and descend only through mismatching child hashes until reaching differing ranges. Matching subtrees need no record transfer, assuming equivalent tree construction and snapshot scope.

cards.prompt: Why must anti-entropy repair preserve tombstones?
cards.answer: An offline replica may retain an older value after another replica deletes it. Without retained deletion metadata and version rules, repair can copy the old value back and resurrect it.

cards.prompt: Why can two correct implementations repeatedly disagree on root hashes?
cards.answer: They may hash different snapshot generations, ranges, record orders or encodings. Agree on deterministic construction and stable comparison scope, then separately handle subsequent writes.
